commit.message:
fix(web): the desk stops disappearing the moment you use it

There were two renders: a desk, and — the instant you clicked Write an order — a
different screen where the desk no longer existed. Fixing the nav last time
stopped the bar changing identity, but the ticket you had just used still
vanished and something else took its place. That is a page change however it is
dressed, and it is what kept feeling wrong.

One render now. The desk is permanent and the trade appears beneath it, so the
page grows instead of swapping: the ticket stays where you left it, the book
keeps taking other people's orders while yours settles, and nothing you were
looking at is taken away.

The ticket does not go grey and empty either — it keeps its content and simply
stops inviting a second order while one is running, because two live invitations
to trade on one screen is its own kind of confusing.

The asset-receipts panel now shows only on an idle desk. During a trade it would
push the thing you are actually watching further down the page.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): the deleted seat still had windows into it

The one-click seat was removed from the door for proving nothing about a
counterparty, but both flows kept buttons that switched back into it — "Run the
one-click demo", "Switch to one-click demo", and, on the screen where a maker
has just lost their bond, "See a settlement that completes". The seat was gone
and its windows were not.

Every one of those renders only when onSwitchToOneClick is supplied, so the
console simply stops supplying it. The one on the expired-payment panel was
unguarded and is deleted outright: it was a dead control offering an escape from
the exact outcome the escrow is built to produce, and the copy beside it now
describes that outcome instead of pointing at a demo.

DeskEntry.tsx goes too — DeskHome replaced it and nothing imported it any more.
Two comments still described the desk as opening on a seat picker; they now
describe what the state actually means, because a comment that lies about a
deleted file is worse than no comment.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): stop the desk turning into a different app when you act

Clicking "Write an order" teleported you somewhere else, and the nav was the
worst of it: "Desk" became "Trade | Make markets" the instant you acted, so the
bar changed identity and the app appeared to become another app. That was the
seat picker returning under a new name. There is one destination now — you are
on the desk either way, and writing or quoting an order is something you do
here, not somewhere you go.

The book had also been wedged in as a third column beside each flow's existing
right-hand rail, which left three columns of chrome and a cramped book. It now
sits full width above the trade, so it stays legible and the flow below keeps
the width it was built for.

Two more things that made the transition read as a glitch: balances appeared
twice, once tidy in the shell and once as the chain's raw float
(198.349284699998) in the rail — both are formatted now — and tokens carried no
mark in the account bar. The mark is the one we already drew for the rail rather
than an official logo, which is someone else's trademark.

Adds Flare's own faucet to the shell, top right. We cannot mint FAssets FXRP
and C2FLR from the source costs the desk nothing, so pointing at the real one is
both honest and better for the visitor.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(web): the book stays on screen while your trade runs

Starting a trade replaced the entire screen, so the desk vanished the moment you
acted on it — which is the shape of a wizard, not a venue. The book now sits
beside the running trade instead of behind it, so other people's orders keep
arriving in front of you while your own settles. That is what a desk looks like,
and it is also the claim the product makes.

OpenOrdersBook is now one component used in both places rather than two copies
that could drift, and it takes a compact flag: the explanatory empty state earns
its space on an idle desk and is noise beside an active trade.

What this does NOT do, stated plainly: the two settlement flows underneath are
still separate state machines with their own consoles. Merging those is a real
rewrite of ~3000 lines that have settled end to end three times, and doing it
two days before feature freeze would risk the only thing that demonstrably
works. The screen is one desk; the plumbing under it is not yet one flow.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: answer the Confidential Compute rubric where a judge will look for it

Bounty 2 names its own grading questions — what runs privately in the TEE, what
the chain verifies, what the trust assumptions are, and why this needs an
enclave rather than a normal contract. The README answered all four, scattered
across five sections. Now it answers them in one, in that order.

The last one is the argument the project actually rests on: anything on-chain is
public, so a sealed-bid market whose bids sit in contract storage is not sealed.
And the property that follows — a losing quote recorded nowhere, not even the
fact that it existed — is one a venue that shows the taker a list cannot offer.

The trust section names the limits without softening them: simulated TEE, no
hardware attestation, a key that regenerates on restart, one enclave we run,
and an owner who can pause locks. It also draws the boundary that matters — the
price band, the drops arithmetic, the payment proof and the bond slash are all
enforced on-chain, so the enclave's power stops at choosing who matches whom.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: receipts for a two-party trade whose taker the contract stamped

Re-ran the two-party settlement end to end now that RFQ submission goes back
through WhisperDeskInstructionSender, and the tables carry that run. It adds the
row the earlier ones could not: submitRfq sent from the taker's own wallet, with
SealedRfqSubmitted naming 0x45712Bef — a wallet created ninety seconds earlier —
as taker, written by the contract rather than supplied by anyone.

Everything else held: the enclave acked the onchain instruction, the order
appeared in the shared book, a maker quoting blind at 1.037674 filled a limit of
1.032557, the XRP landed on the taker's own XRPL account, and release() moved
1.0 FXRP to the maker. Desk on neither side.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: correct the 404 diagnosis — it was our registration, not Flare's proxy

Four pages said onchain instructions were unreachable because Flare's hosted
FTDC proxy answered our availability check with a 404, and called that a routing
failure outside our contracts. That was wrong, and blaming a third party for our
own misconfiguration is the kind of wrong worth correcting loudly.

Our TEE machine was registered on-chain under http://localhost:6674. Flare's
data providers push to the URL recorded on-chain, so they were pushing at a
loopback address that meant nothing to them, and the availability check could
never complete. updateTeeMachineSettings corrected it, the machine reached
PRODUCTION, and an onchain submitRfq returned an enclave ack on the first try.

The pages now describe the shipped behaviour — orders sealed by the desk and
submitted from the taker's own wallet, so the taker is stamped from msg.sender
rather than claimed — and carry the debugging note that cost us the most time:
register-tee will not update that URL for an already-registered machine whatever
flags you pass, because Register() is its only writer and it gets skipped. Other
teams are stuck on exactly this.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat: the taker is stamped by the contract again, not self-attested

Every onchain submitRfq had been 404ing, so RFQ_SUBMIT moved to POST /direct
where the taker rides in the envelope and is merely claimed. I attributed that
404 to Flare's hosted proxy and wrote it into the README that way. It was ours:
our TEE machine was registered under `http://localhost:6674`, and Flare's data
providers push to the URL recorded on-chain, so they were pushing at a loopback
address that meant nothing to them.

updateTeeMachineSettings corrected the URL — no re-registration, no new
extension id, no key rotation — and the machine reached PRODUCTION. Proven
before any of this code changed: an onchain submitRfq returned an enclave ack
with status 1, the contract stamping our wallet as taker (tx 0xe57cb5ff…128e,
rfqId 0xbdfd61f3…264f).

So submission goes back through WhisperDeskInstructionSender, from the taker's
own wallet. /publish now seals and returns the ciphertext instead of sending it,
because the whole point is that the desk must NOT be the sender; /confirm reads
the receipt, checks the stamped taker against the address claiming to have sent
it, and publishes the rfqId into the shared book.

RFQ_MATCH stays on /direct deliberately. It is permissionless on either ingress,
carries no secret, and names no party, so onchain would add a transaction, a fee
and a wait to a call anyone may make.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): stop the desk re-rendering an empty book once a second

The countdown ticker ran unconditionally, so a desk with nothing on it still
re-rendered every second forever. The page never reached document idle — which
is how it surfaced, since tooling that waits for idle simply timed out — and on
a phone it would have burned battery animating nothing. It now runs only while
there is a countdown to move.

Also: the receipts paragraph was the only flexible child on its row, so it
collapsed to its 24ch floor and read as a narrow gutter beside the links; a real
basis gives it a readable measure and wraps the receipts below instead. And the
copy still said "every seat here settles" — the word the seats were removed to
get rid of.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(web): one desk, no seats — and the wallet gates content, not the door

The console opened on a full-page chooser asking whether you were the taker or
the maker. No exchange asks that. You do not tell a swap venue whether you are
a liquidity provider; you take an action and the role follows. Asking first
made the product explain a concept it should have been demonstrating, and it
put a splash in front of an application nobody had been shown yet.

DeskHome replaces it with what a desk actually shows: a ticket to write an
order, and the book of orders already open. Write one and you are the taker.
Quote one and you are the maker. Those two words now appear only where they
describe what already happened.

The book is public and polls whether or not a wallet is attached — an empty
desk and a desk you are not allowed to see are different things, and only one
is honest. The gate sits on the actions that need a signature, inside the
shell, which stays visible throughout. What the book shows is deliberately just
an id and a countdown: size, limit, side and author stay in the enclave, and a
book that listed them would be an order book rather than a dark one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): format the account figures and stop stacking two identities

Two defects visible the moment the shell rendered against a real wallet. C2FLR
read 198.349284699998 — the chain's float forwarded verbatim, which is the tell
that a screen relays data rather than presenting it; four decimals is enough to
watch gas move and few enough to read at a glance. And "WhisperDesk" appeared
twice, once in the page header and again in the shell, so the bar competed with
the header directly above it. The shell keeps the mark and drops the wordmark.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(web): give the desk an application shell instead of a bare panel

The working surface had no chrome of its own — no brand, no destinations, no
network, no account, no session. A visitor met a lone panel above a log, which
is why it read as a guided demo however the buttons were worded. Relabelling
was never going to fix that; the structure was the problem.

AppShell answers the four questions every dapp answers before anything is
clicked, in a bar that then stays put: where am I, what can I do here, which
chain, which account. The two seats become destinations named Trade and Make
markets rather than a segmented control, because a stage implies an order and a
finish while a destination is somewhere you can leave and come back to.

The account sits in a rule-separated band, not a row of stat cards: a desk
shows its account the way a terminal does — dense, tabular, on one line — and
that keeps the figures subordinate to the work. Switching is still blocked
mid-settlement, where leaving would strand an open match.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: say that the taker writes the order, and show the bounds refusing bad ones

The receipts described a two-party trade without mentioning who chose its terms,
which was fair when the desk chose them and is wrong now that it does not. Both
pages carry the run where the taker picked 1.0 FXRP at a limit of 1.030323 and a
maker filled it quoting 1.035118, plus the three rejections that prove the bounds
are enforced rather than advisory.

Also states where those bounds come from, since that is the load-bearing part:
MIN_BLOCK_FXRP off the escrow and mid x (1 + BAND_BIPS) off FTSOv2, each read
from the contract that enforces it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): stop steering the maker into letting the desk hold their key

The XRP leg offered two routes and led with the wrong one. "Fund a throwaway
XRPL account for me" settles in seconds against a 180-second payment window,
which is a real advantage and why it led — but this server generates and holds
that account's seed. A desk holding one side's payment key is not a third
party, whatever the escrow enforces.

Paying from your own wallet leads now, since that is what a real maker does and
the escrow credits the payment however it arrives. The throwaway stays for
anyone who wants it, relabelled so the custody is stated rather than implied.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat: the taker writes the order, the desk only seals it

The desk composed every published RFQ itself — side, size and limit were all
server-side constants and the visitor supplied nothing but two addresses. That
still hid the order from makers, which is the part that matters commercially,
but it made "the desk cannot read your order" a hollow sentence: nothing is
hidden from the party that wrote it. A venue that authors your order is not a
third party.

GET /api/taker/rfq/prepare now returns the bounds instead of a fixed amount,
and each one is read from the system that enforces it rather than asserted —
MIN_BLOCK_FXRP off the escrow (the enclave's AddRFQ rejects below it and lock()
rejects below it), and mid * (1 + BAND_BIPS) off FTSOv2 plus the escrow, which
is the highest limit any quote could legally clear. The taker states size and
limit inside those bounds; publish re-checks both and answers 400 naming the
bound that was missed, rather than spending a sealing round trip to earn an
opaque WD_ERR_.

Verified live: an order below the block minimum, one above the band, and a zero
limit are each refused with the reason. Then a full settlement on an order the
taker chose — 1.0 FXRP at a limit of 1.0303, filled by a maker quoting 1.0351,
taker 0x6e6F7743, release 0x2da3adc2.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): the door still promised the desk on the other side of every trade

Two stale claims on the seat picker, found by reading the rendered page rather
than the source. It offered "the no-setup seat" as the wallet-free alternative,
which was deleted; and it said the desk takes the other side of whichever seat
you pick, full stop. That second one is the sentence this whole change set
exists to stop being true.

Both halves are stated now: the desk does stand in by default, and publishing
to the open desk takes it out of the trade entirely.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: point the receipts at the run the published script actually produces

The first two-party settlement was real, but the script aborted after the match
on an assertion of mine that decoded matches() with the wrong field order —
it is packed for storage, so destinationTag/lockedAt/state sit between taker
and maker. The trade was fine; my check was not. Settlement was finished by
hand that time.

The ABI is now copied verbatim from abi.ts rather than retyped, and the script
has since run start to finish unattended with a different fresh taker. The
tables now carry that run, because it is the one a judge following the README
will reproduce. The first run stays cited: two unrelated takers settling the
same evening says more about reproducibility than either run alone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): the desk cannot mint an asset that has no mint

The maker seat still failed after the /direct migration, and not because of
routing: opening an RFQ called mint() on the FXRP token. That worked when the
token was MockFXRP and has been dead since both escrows were redeployed against
genuine FAssets FXRP, which has no privileged supply — it exists only against
XRP locked in FAssets. The failure surfaced as an unknown selector inside
estimateGas (0x6d5ab9d3), which is about as unhelpful as errors get.

Three call sites had the same leftover: fundTakerDeposit, fundMakerBond, and
both faucet routes. They now move FXRP the desk already holds, and say so
plainly when the reserve is dry instead of reverting.

Funding also stopped being unconditional. An escrow deposit is not consumed by
opening an RFQ — it is reserved at lock() and comes back on release or refund —
so re-depositing on every call was draining a reserve that cannot be minted
back. Both helpers now top up only the shortfall, and when the balance is
already sufficient but its arming window has run short, deposit(0, …) extends
it for free.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: two strangers settled a block, and say what the ingress now costs

Adds the receipts for the run that finally proves the product rather than
the machinery: a taker wallet generated during the run, a maker who never
saw the order, and a desk holding neither leg. Every prior receipt in the
README and GitBook had the desk on one side of the trade.

Also corrects a claim that had gone stale in five places. "Two RFQ ingresses
exist, and both work" is no longer true — the onchain one routes through
Flare's hosted FTDC proxy, which answers our machine-availability check with
a 404. The contract half is still deployed, registry-enforced and proven, so
the pages say that, and then say plainly that the live site runs on /direct
with a self-attested taker.

The cost of that is stated precisely everywhere it appears, because vagueness
here would be the dishonest part: it costs attribution, not safety. lock()
reserves the FXRP from the named taker's own armed deposit and pays the XRP to
the address sealed beside it, so naming someone else either settles the trade
to them or cannot lock at all. RFQ_MATCH over /direct costs nothing at all.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat: the two seats meet without the desk between them

The taker seat published its RFQ through WhisperDeskInstructionSender, and the
maker seat triggered matching the same way. Both routed through Flare's hosted
FTDC proxy, which now answers the machine-availability check with a 404, so
neither seat could reach the enclave — the one path where two independent
people end up on one trade was the one that was down.

Both commands move to POST /direct. The cost is not symmetric and the code says
so in both places: RFQ_MATCH loses nothing (permissionless either way, carries
no secret, names no party), while RFQ_SUBMIT loses the msg.sender stamp and the
taker becomes self-attested. What that does not open up is enforced rather than
trusted — lock() reserves the fill from the named taker's own armed deposit and
pays the XRP to the address sealed beside it, so naming someone else either
settles the trade to them or cannot lock at all.

The desk now seals, relays, and pays gas for two permissionless calls. It holds
neither leg of a published trade.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): trim the rail so the desk fits one screen

Three stacked panels — market reference, auction rule, holdings — each carried
a multi-line footnote, and together they pushed the maker seat well past the
fold. A trading screen that needs scrolling to see the price and the position
is not doing its job.

Each footnote is now one line. The arguments they were making still exist in
full; they live in the docs, where there is room for them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(web): drop the no-setup seat

It ran both sides of the trade from the desk's own keys. That demonstrated the
machinery — DvP, FDC proof, real FAssets FXRP — but proved nothing about a
counterparty, and a judge watching it could not tell whether anyone
independent was ever involved. Two seats remain, and each puts a real wallet
on one side.

The wallet-aware default that silently rerouted a wallet-less visitor into
that tab goes with it. DeskEntry already says "No wallet in this browser" on
the card rather than moving someone to a seat they did not pick.

Verified live: the door now offers exactly "Sit as the taker" and "Sit as the
maker".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: the mock is gone, so stop apologising for it

Every page still explained why the demo settled a stand-in and offered two
settlements elsewhere as proof the mechanism was not mock-bound. None of that
is true any more: both escrows settle FAssets FXRP and there is nothing to
apologise for.

README, GitBook and the live panels now say what happens — every seat settles
the genuine asset, visitors fund themselves from Flare's faucet, nobody can
mint it because it only exists against XRP locked in FAssets. The address
tables carry the new escrows and BondLedgers, and the roadmap's FAssets row
moved from "settle the demo in real FXRP" to wiring mint/redeem into the desk,
which is what is actually left.

The receipts panel on /demo kept its links and gained a third: the run that
retired the mock, on the escrow the demo now uses.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat: the desk settles real FAssets FXRP — the mock is gone

Flare's own faucet hands out 10 FXRP per address per day. That single fact
removed the only reason MockFXRP ever existed: the demo faucet had to fund
every visitor, and real FXRP could not be conjured per visitor. It can now be
requested, so it is.

Two escrows redeployed against the genuine asset (0x0b6A3645…3dc7), because
the two paths need different signers and one contract cannot be both:
  open-desk 0xB3C7626…044C — teeSigner is the live enclave, for sealed matching
  one-click 0x7876873…fB5c — teeSigner is the owner, which self-signs its match

Verified the enclave key still derives to 0x5656…c18B before deploying, so the
new escrow trusts a key that is actually running rather than a rotated ghost.

The mint button is gone with the mock. Nothing we run can create FAssets FXRP —
it exists only against XRP locked in FAssets, which is precisely what makes it
worth settling. Holdings links to Flare's faucet instead, and the label it
briefly got wrong is now simply true.

Desk wallets funded from the 28 FXRP the owner held.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): Holdings called a mock token FAssets

The panel labelled every FXRP balance "FAssets · Coston2". It is MockFXRP — a
mintable test token the faucet prints on demand. The mislabel survived because
the mock's symbol also reads FXRP; the genuine FAssets asset is FTestXRP at
0x0b6A3645…3dc7, on a separate escrow, and is never what this panel shows.

Caught by a reader asking which one it actually was, which is the right
question to ask of any panel claiming provenance.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(web): send people to Flare's faucet for gas, not to the desk's reserve

Coston2 gas is free from faucet.flare.network, so paying for it out of the
desk's own key was buying nothing. Worse, it was the same key that funds every
settlement the desk runs — each visitor topped up here was reserve unavailable
to finish a trade, and the owner balance had already moved 30.75 to 29.25
doing it.

Flare's faucet is now the primary action. The drip survives underneath as a
quiet second line, because the case it was built for is still real: running
dry mid-run, where sending someone off-site is how a judge abandons the demo
rather than finishes it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): publish to the open desk mints the open desk's own token

"MockFXRP: insufficient balance" — with a balance sitting in the Holdings rail
two inches away. The open-desk path settles on the enclave-loop escrow, which
has its own MockFXRP (0xBc224256…), while Holdings mints the demo escrow's.
Judges arrived holding the wrong token and had no way to tell, because both
are called FXRP and both show up as a number in the same panel.

The publish flow now tops up the correct token before depositing it. A 429
there means an earlier run already left some, which is success.

The rate limiter made it worse: both faucets shared one map, so claiming the
demo token burned your claim on the one you actually needed — the exact dead
end hit in testing, where the retry was refused for ten minutes. They now
count separately, which is what they always should have done given they mint
different contracts.

Found by running it, not by reading it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): a JSX comment took the site down

The console placeholder fix shipped with a `{/* … */}` comment inside a
ternary branch. A JSX comment is itself an expression, so the branch held two
children with no fragment around them and the parse failed.

The build failed. The deploy did not: `npm run build | grep … | head` returns
head's exit status, so `&&` saw success and shipped an incomplete .next. The
site returned 502 — during a live test, which is where the "XRPL payment
failed" and "match() failed" lines in that run came from.

Rolled back to the previous build to restore service, then fixed the comment
and redeployed behind an explicit exit check that refuses to package anything
if the build did not succeed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(web): the console stopped waiting for a step that no longer exists

Both consoles opened on "Waiting for step 1…", left behind when the numbered
badges came out. A terminal that names a step is describing a wizard, and this
one had already stopped being either.

Swept the rest of the user-facing copy for the same rot: everything else is
comments, or DvpFlow on the landing page, where "Step 01 / 06" is a narrated
walkthrough and belongs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(web): panels, not a numbered wizard

With only the current stage rendered, the numeral on each badge answered a
question nobody was asking — "which of seven forms am I on" — and made a
trading desk read like onboarding. A live dot or a tick says what a terminal
says instead: this is happening, or this is done. The ordinal survives as
data-stage in the DOM, which is the only reader that ever wanted it.

Headers now match every other panel on the page — ice label, ruled divider,
padded body — so the work area stops looking like a different component family
from the rail beside it.

Titles name the action rather than the position in a queue: "Your receive
address", "Open the trade", "Settlement"; "Take a request", "Your quote".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(web): say why nobody gets to pick the fill

Not offering a taker a list of quotes to choose from reads as a missing
feature until the reason is on screen. It is the opposite: the rule runs
inside the enclave, so nobody can steer it — not the desk operating the venue,
not the taker who wrote the order, not a maker with a relationship to lean on.
Best price wins because a deterministic function said so, somewhere no one can
reach.

The second half is the part a pick-your-quote venue cannot match. Showing a
taker the list means disclosing every loser to someone. Here a quote that
clears all six filters and simply loses on price is recorded nowhere — not in
the match response, not in the aggregate reasons map. Losing costs a maker
nothing, not even the fact that they turned up.

Static on purpose. Wiring this panel to a live figure would invite the one
number it must never carry: how many others are quoting.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(web): put the request queue where a dealer desk keeps it

Three columns on the maker seat, matching how a dealer terminal actually
reads: the flow of requests on the left, the thing you are doing in the
middle, standing context on the right. The queue was buried inside the first
step, which meant the market only appeared once you had already started your
own paperwork — backwards for a desk whose whole point is that other people's
orders arrive.

Rows carry an id and a status and nothing else. That is not restraint for its
own sake: a side or a size in this list would hand a maker the very fields the
enclave exists to seal.

Below xl the third column would stop being readable, so it collapses and the
queue folds back inline rather than vanishing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(web): the two seats finally meet

A taker can now publish their own sealed RFQ into the shared queue instead of
trading against the house, and a maker in another window can fill it. That
closes the loop the demo never had: until now every path had the desk on one
side, so no run ever put two independent people on one trade.

The flow is approve, deposit, submitRfq — all three from the judge's own
wallet. submitRfq especially: the sender contract stamps the taker from
msg.sender, so relaying it from a desk key would forge the very identity the
on-chain ingress exists to protect. The server seals the ciphertext and reads
back the receipt; it never sends the transaction.

fix(competing-makers): five real bugs, found by running it

The script landed unexecuted last commit. Running it surfaced five defects,
each fixed against the actual source rather than by guessing again:

- Binary path was relative while execFileSync sets cwd=clientDir, so the path
  resolved against the new cwd. Absolute now, with the .exe suffix Windows
  needs for a full path.
- ABI was invented: instructionId is bytes32 (not uint256) and MatchTriggered
  carries a third indexed topic. Wrong types make parseLog silently skip the
  event, which surfaced as "SealedRfqSubmitted not emitted".
- Result polling went through wd-client's `result` subcommand, which takes the
  id positionally and cannot filter by submission tag. Replaced with the HTTP
  poll onchain-loop.mjs already uses in production — and hardened: the proxy
  returns a `result` envelope before the enclave writes a payload into it, so
  waiting on `result` alone races the enclave and yields empty data.
- RFQ payload used `xrplTakerAddress`; the enclave's wire contract
  (extension/fcewire/wire.go) says `xrplAddress`.
- The RFQ was submitted by the relayer. WhisperDeskInstructionSender stamps the
  taker from msg.sender and the enclave requires the payload's taker to equal
  that envelope sender — anything else is WD_ERR_AUTH, which is the ingress
  doing its job. Submitted by the taker now, with an assertion on the stamped
  address so a future regression fails at the cause.
